title: Double Take on the Ballot: Inside the Long, Dirty History of 'Ghost Candidates'
snippet: From three Bob Fergusons in Washington to duplicate Dan Sullivans in Alaska, political operatives have long used same-name spoiler candidates to trick voters—a deceptive tactic pushing the boundaries of election law.
content:
When voters in Washington state prepared to cast their primary ballots for governor, they didn't just see one Bob Ferguson listed under the Democratic column—they saw three. The state's attorney general, a prominent Democrat, suddenly found himself sharing the ballot with two political novices who shared his exact name, secretly recruited and funded by a conservative activist hoping to split the vote.

While those decoy Fergusons quickly dropped out under threat of legal action, the scheme of planting same-name candidates is far from an isolated glitch. In fact, it remains one of American politics' oldest and most cynical campaign tricks, currently taking center stage in a high-stakes Alaska U.S. Senate clash between incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and a political newcomer named Daniel J. Sullivan.

A Century-Old Tradition of Voter Confusion

Using decoy candidates to siphon votes away from frontrunners is a strategy stretching back nearly a century. In 1930, legendary Nebraska Senator George W. Norris faced a Republican primary threat from a local grocery clerk who happened to be named George W. Norris. The incumbent narrowly avoided political disaster only when state officials disqualified the clerk's petition over a filing deadline technicality.

Sometimes, same-name candidates aren't even planted by opposition operatives—they simply capitalize on famous names for personal gain. In 1954, a Gillette razor factory stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy entered the race for Massachusetts state treasurer. Riding entirely on the coattails and name recognition of then-U.S. Senator John Fitzgerald Kennedy, the high school dropout won the statewide election without launching a single formal campaign event, ultimately serving three terms.

Where Election Strategy Crosses into Criminality

Because citizens generally hold a constitutional right to run for public office under their legal names, proving that a candidacy is an illegal fraud presents a steep legal challenge. However, operatives cross into criminal territory when financial payoffs, campaign finance violations, or residency fraud enter the picture.

In 2020, former Florida state Sen. Frank Artiles was convicted after orchestrating a $50,000 scheme to recruit a 'ghost candidate' named Alex Rodriguez. That decoy managed to draw over 6,000 votes, allowing the Republican challenger to unseat Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez by a razor-thin 32-vote margin.

To combat similar tactics in Washington state, Attorney General Bob Ferguson leveraged an obscure 1933 law making it a felony to file under a duplicate name with the explicit intent to mislead electors. The legal threat forced his political namesakes off the ballot within 72 hours.

Alaska's High-Stakes Battleground

The latest fight over duplicate names has unfolded in Alaska, where Republicans have accused Democrats of backing retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to undercut incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan. The controversy ignited national backlash, leading to a preemptive Department of Justice lawsuit and calls from former President Donald Trump for criminal investigations.

Despite the legal drama, experts emphasize that Alaska's unique ranked-choice voting system provides built-in insurance against such hijinks. Because Alaskans can rank multiple preferences on a single ballot, confused voters can rank both Sullivans, largely neutralizing the impact of one of the oldest dirty tricks in American political history.
